derivations.claim: The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$. For $n=0$ the Grassmannian is a point and $H^*=\mathbb F_2$ by [F1], with no positive classes. For $n=1$ the Grassmannian is $\mathbb{RP}^\infty$, so [F6] gives $H^*=\mathbb F_2[a]=\mathbb F_2[w_1(\gamma_1)]$ because $w_1(\gamma_1)=a$; this is the assertion for $n=1$. [F1, F6]

The sphere bundle and its total space. For $n\geq2$ let $\pi:S(\gamma_n)\to B\operatorname O(n)$ be the unit sphere bundle of $\gamma_n$, a numerable fiber bundle with fiber $S^{n-1}$, and consider $p:S(\gamma_n)\to B\operatorname O(n-1)=\operatorname{Gr}_{n-1}(\mathbb R^\infty)$, $(W,v)\mapsto W\cap v^{\perp}$, the orthogonal complement of $v$ in the $n$-plane $W$. In a local frame of $\gamma_n$ this is the map $U\times S^{n-1}\to\operatorname{Gr}_{n-1}(\mathbb R^\infty)$ obtained by orthogonally completing the frame; it is a numerable fiber bundle whose fiber over an $(n-1)$-plane $P$ is the unit sphere in $P^{\perp}\cong\mathbb R^\infty$, that is $S^\infty$. Since $B\operatorname O(n-1)$ is a path-connected CW complex by [F1], the spectral sequence [F4] has $E_2^{a,b}=H^a(B\operatorname O(n-1);\mathcal H^b)$ with $\mathcal H^b=0$ for $b>0$ and $\mathcal H^0=\mathbb F_2$ constant by [F5], so the sequence is concentrated in the row $b=0$ and the edge map $p^*:H^k(B\operatorname O(n-1);\mathbb F_2)\to H^k(S(\gamma_n);\mathbb F_2)$ is an isomorphism for every $k$. [F1, F4, F5]

The pullback of the tautological bundle splits. Let $L\subseteq\pi^*\gamma_n$ be the vertical line bundle, whose fiber over $(W,v)$ is the line $\mathbb R v$; it is trivialized by the section $(W,v)\mapsto(W,v,v)$. Orthogonal projection with respect to a metric on $\pi^*\gamma_n$ splits $\pi^*\gamma_n\cong L\oplus p^*\gamma_{n-1}$, because the fiber of $p^*\gamma_{n-1}$ over $(W,v)$ is $W\cap v^{\perp}$. Therefore, by [F7], the total class is multiplicative, $$w(\pi^*\gamma_n)=w(L)\,w(p^*\gamma_{n-1})=w(p^*\gamma_{n-1}),$$ since the trivial line bundle $L$ has total class $1$; comparing components of this identity gives $w_j(\pi^*\gamma_n)=w_j(p^*\gamma_{n-1})=p^*w_j(\gamma_{n-1})$ for every $j$. [F7, step 1.2]

The map $\eta$ and surjectivity. Define $\eta:H^*(B\operatorname O(n);\mathbb F_2)\to H^*(B\operatorname O(n-1);\mathbb F_2)$ as the composite of $\pi^*$ with the inverse of the isomorphism $p^*$ of step 1.2. Then step 2.1 gives $\eta(w_j(\gamma_n))=w_j(\gamma_{n-1})$ for every $j$, with the convention $w_n(\gamma_{n-1})=0$. Assume now, as induction hypothesis, that $H^*(B\operatorname O(n-1);\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1}]$ with $w_j=w_j(\gamma_{n-1})$. Then the image of $\eta$ contains all polynomial generators of $H^*(B\operatorname O(n-1);\mathbb F_2)$ and hence is everything: $\eta$ is surjective. [step 1.2, step 2.1]

The Gysin sequence breaks into short exact sequences. The mod-two Gysin sequence of [F3] for $\xi=\gamma_n$ is $$\cdots\to H^{k-n}(B\operatorname O(n))\xrightarrow{\smile e_2}H^k(B\operatorname O(n))\xrightarrow{\pi^*}H^k(S(\gamma_n))\xrightarrow{\partial_G}H^{k-n+1}(B\operatorname O(n))\to\cdots,$$ and identifying the middle term with $H^k(B\operatorname O(n-1))$ through step 1.2 turns $\pi^*$ into $\eta$. Since $\eta$ is surjective by step 3.1, exactness gives short exact sequences $$0\to H^{i}(B\operatorname O(n))\xrightarrow{\smile e_2}H^{i+n}(B\operatorname O(n))\xrightarrow{\eta}H^{i+n}(B\operatorname O(n-1))\to0$$ for every $i$. In particular $\smile e_2:H^i\to H^{i+n}$ is injective for every $i$. [F3, step 1.2, step 3.1, F2]

Identification of the Euler class with $w_n$. Take $k=n$ and $i=0$ in step 4.1: the image of $\smile e_2:H^0(B\operatorname O(n))\to H^n(B\operatorname O(n))$ is a one-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-space generated by $e_2(\gamma_n)$, and it equals the kernel of $\eta$ in degree $n$. That kernel contains $w_n(\gamma_n)$, since $\eta(w_n(\gamma_n))=w_n(\gamma_{n-1})=0$ by step 3.1. Moreover $w_n(\gamma_n)\neq0$: let $f:\mathbb{RP}^\infty\to B\operatorname O(n)$ be a classifying map of the $n$-fold sum $\gamma_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\gamma_1$ of the universal line, which exists by [F8]; then $f^*w_n(\gamma_n)=w_n(f^*\gamma_n)=(w_1(\gamma_1))^n=a^n\neq0$ by the Whitney formula [F7] and [F6]. 3.1 The conjugation formula. Let $q=a+r$ be a unit quaternion, with real $a$ and imaginary $r$; put $s=\lVert r\rVert_2$ and, when $s>0$, $u=r/s$. For imaginary $w$ orthogonal to $u$, expanding $(a+su)w(a-su)$ by distributivity and using $uw=-wu$ and $uwu=w$ from step 2.1 gives $qw\bar q=(a^2-s^2)w+2as\,uw$, while expanding $(a+su)(uw)(a-su)$ and using $u(uw)=-w$ gives $q(uw)\bar q=(a^2-s^2)uw-2as\,w$; also $qu\bar q=(a^2+s^2)u=u$, because $u^2=-1$ and $a^2+s^2=N(q)=1$. Writing $C=a^2-s^2$ and $S=2as$, the identity $C^2+S^2=(a^2+s^2)^2=1$ holds and will be used below; conjugation by $q$ is linear in its argument and preserves the imaginary subspace, so $\rho(q)$ is a well-defined endomorphism of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$, and for $s=0$, that is for $q=\pm1$, it is the identity. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 The action of $R$ on the plane orthogonal to its axis. Keep $R\ne I$ and the unit fixed vector $u$ of step 1.3, and choose a unit $w$ orthogonal to $u$; by step 2.1 the list $(u,w,uw)$ is an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$. By [F4] the map $R$ preserves inner products, so $Ru=u$, the vector $Rw$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $u$, and $R(uw)$ is a unit vector orthogonal to both $u$ and $Rw$. In the orthonormal basis $(w,uw)$ of the plane orthogonal to $u$ we may therefore write $Rw=(\cos\theta)w+(\sin\theta)uw$ for exactly one $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ by [F7], while $R(uw)=\varepsilon(-(\sin\theta)w+(\cos\theta)uw)$ for a sign $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, those being the two unit vectors orthogonal to $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. The matrix of $R$ in the ordered basis $(u,w,uw)$ therefore has columns $(1,0,0)$, $(0,\cos\theta,-\varepsilon\sin\theta)$ and $(0,\sin\theta,\varepsilon\cos\theta)$, and the Leibniz formula of [F5] gives its determinant as $\varepsilon(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=\varepsilon$; since determinants are basis-independent by [F5] and $\det R=1$, we conclude $\varepsilon=1$. [F4, F5, F7, F2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The map $\rho(q)$ preserves norms. For $v\in\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ write $v=cu+w$ with $c=\langle v,u\rangle$ real and $w$ orthogonal to $u$, so that $\lVert v\rVert_2^2=c^2+\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ by [F3]; by linearity of conjugation by $q$ and the identities of step 3.1, $qv\bar q=cu+Cw+S\,uw$. The three summands are pairwise orthogonal, and $\lVert uw\rVert_2=\lVert w\rVert_2$ by step 2.1, so the squared norm is $c^2+C^2\lVert w\rVert_2^2+S^2\lVert w\rVert_2^2=c^2+\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ by [F3] and $C^2+S^2=1$. Hence $\lVert qv\bar q\rVert_2=\lVert v\rVert_2$ for all $v$, and the same holds for $q=\pm1$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The map $\rho$ is surjective. For $R=I$ we have $R=\rho(1)$. For $R\ne I$ keep $u$, $w$, $\theta$ from step 3.2 and put $q_0=\cos(\theta/2)+\sin(\theta/2)u$, a unit quaternion by [F7]. The addition formulas of [F7] with equal arguments give $\cos\theta=\cos^2(\theta/2)-\sin^2(\theta/2)$ and $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$, so step 3.1 applied to $q_0$, whose imaginary part has norm $\sin(\theta/2)$ and direction $u$, gives $\rho(q_0)(u)=u$, $\rho(q_0)(w)=(\cos\theta)w+(\sin\theta)uw$ and $\rho(q_0)(uw)=(\cos\theta)uw-(\sin\theta)w$. By step 3.2 these values agree with those of $R$ on the basis $(u,w,uw)$, and two linear maps with equal values on a basis are equal by [F3]. Hence $R=\rho(q_0)$ and $\rho$ is onto. [F3, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The image of $\rho$ lies in $\operatorname{SO}(3)$. By step 4.1 the endomorphism $\rho(q)$ preserves norms, so by [F4] it preserves inner products, satisfies $\rho(q)^*\rho(q)=I$ and is invertible, and its matrix in the orthonormal basis $(i,j,k)$ satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}R=I$ by [F4]. In the orthonormal basis $(u,w,uw)$ of step 2.1 the identities of step 3.1 show that the columns of the matrix of $\rho(q)$ are $(1,0,0)$, $(0,C,S)$ and $(0,-S,C)$; in the Leibniz formula of [F5] for this matrix only the identity permutation and one transposition contribute, giving determinant $C^2+S^2=1$. Determinants of endomorphisms may be computed in any ordered basis by [F5], so $\det\rho(q)=1$ and $\rho(q)\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$; for $q=\pm1$ the endomorphism is the identity. Thus $\rho$ is a well-defined map $S^3\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$. [F4, F5, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The map $\rho$ is a homomorphism with kernel $\{\pm1\}$. For unit $q_1,q_2$, associativity of multiplication gives $(q_1q_2)v(q_1q_2)^{-1}=q_1(q_2vq_2^{-1})q_1^{-1}$, that is $\rho(q_1q_2)=\rho(q_1)\rho(q_2)$, and $\rho(1)$ is the identity. If $\rho(q)$ is the identity then $q$ commutes with $i,j,k$: comparing $qi$ with $iq$ in the coordinates of [F1] forces the $j$- and $k$-coefficients of $q$ to vanish, and then comparing $qj$ with $jq$ forces the $i$-coefficient to vanish, so $q$ is real, and being a unit it is $\pm1$; conversely $\pm1$ act trivially. Hence $\ker\rho=\{\pm1\}$, and because $\rho(q^{-1}q')=\rho(q)^{-1}\rho(q')$ we have $\rho(q')=\rho(q)$ exactly when $q'=\pm q$. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 The map $\rho:S^3\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is continuous. By step 2.2 the map $S^3\to\mathbb R^9$ recording the matrix of the endomorphism $v\mapsto qv\bar q$ is continuous, and by step 5.1 that endomorphism is $\rho(q)\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$; since $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ carries the subspace topology of the nine entries, the map $\rho$ into $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is continuous by [F8]. [F8, step 2.2, step 5.1]

7.1 The induced map on the orbit space is a continuous bijection. Let $G=\{\pm1\}$. By step 6.1, $\rho(q')=\rho(q)$ exactly when $q'=\pm q$, so $\rho$ is constant on the orbits of $G$ and its fibres are exactly those orbits; note also that $\rho(-q)=\rho(q)$, since $(-q)v(-q)^{-1}=qvq^{-1}$. Since $\pi$ is a quotient map by [F11] and $\rho$ is continuous by step 6.2, the characteristic property and the factorisation clause of [F11] give a continuous map $\bar\rho:S^3/G\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ with $\bar\rho\circ\pi=\rho$; it is injective because the fibres of $\rho$ are the orbits and it is surjective by step 4.2. [F11, F12, step 2.3, step 4.2, step 6.1, step 6.2]

8.1 The induced map is a homeomorphism. The orbit space $S^3/G$ is compact, being the continuous image under $\pi$ of the compact space $S^3$ by [F9] and step 2.3, and $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is Hausdorff, being a subspace of the nine-dimensional matrix space $\mathbb R^9$ with its product topology, hence metrizable, by [F5] and [F9]. The continuous bijection $\bar\rho$ of step 7.1 is therefore a homeomorphism by the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [F9]. [F9, F5, step 2.3, step 7.1]

9.1 The map $\rho$ is a two-sheeted covering. Let $y\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ and let $V$ be an evenly covered neighbourhood of $\bar\rho^{-1}(y)$ for the covering $\pi$ of step 2.3, so that $\pi^{-1}(V)$ is a disjoint union of open sheets, each mapped homeomorphically onto $V$ by $\pi$; each sheet meets each fibre of $\pi$ in exactly one point, so there are exactly two sheets, the fibres of $\pi$ being the two-point orbits of step 7.1. Put $W=\bar\rho(V)$, which is open by step 8.1. Then $\rho^{-1}(W)=\pi^{-1}(\bar\rho^{-1}(W))=\pi^{-1}(V)$ is a disjoint union of two open sets, and on each of them $\rho$ is the composite of the homeomorphism $\pi$ with the homeomorphism $\bar\rho$, hence a homeomorphism onto $W$. So every point of $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ has an evenly covered neighbourhood with two sheets; $\rho$ is a continuous surjection by step 6.2 and step 4.2, and $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is thereby homeomorphic to $S^3/\{\pm1\}$ through $\bar\rho$. [F12, step 2.3, step 4.2, step 6.2, step 7.1, step 8.1]

10.1 Covering projections induce isomorphisms on higher homotopy groups. By step 1.7 and step 2.4, for every covering $p:E\to B$ and every $n\ge2$ the homomorphism $p_*:\pi_n(E,e_0)\to\pi_n(B,p(e_0))$ is bijective, hence an isomorphism of the groups of [F13]. Applying this to the covering $\rho:S^3\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ of step 9.1 with $e_0=1$, where $\rho(1)=I$, the homomorphism $\rho_*:\pi_3(S^3,1)\to\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)$ is an isomorphism. [F13, step 1.7, step 2.4, step 9.1]

10.2 The map $\rho$ is not nullhomotopic. Suppose $H:S^3\times I\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ were a homotopy with $H_0=\rho$ and $H_1$ constant. The identity map of $S^3$ is a lift of $H_0=\rho$ through the covering $\rho$ of step 9.1, because $\rho\circ\operatorname{id}=\rho$; lifting $H$ by [F12] gives $\widetilde H:S^3\times I\to S^3$ with $\widetilde H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $\rho\circ\widetilde H=H$. The map $\widetilde H_1$ lifts the constant map $H_1$, so its image lies in one fibre of $\rho$, a two-point set; since $S^3$ is connected by [F10], the continuous image $\widetilde H_1(S^3)$ is connected and contained in a set of two points separated in the Hausdorff space $S^3$ by [F9], so $\widetilde H_1$ is constant. Thus the identity of $S^3$ is homotopic to a constant map, and by [F14] those two maps have equal degree, contradicting the values $1$ and $0$ established in step 1.6. Hence $\rho$ is not nullhomotopic. [F12, F14, F10, F9, step 1.6, step 9.1]

11.1 The third homotopy group of $\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Transport the based sphere map $\rho$ to the cubical model through [F13] and write $[\rho]\in\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)$ for its class; since $\rho_*$ is the isomorphism of step 10.1, functoriality in [F13] gives $\rho_*[\operatorname{id}]=[\rho\circ\operatorname{id}]=[\rho]$ for the generator $[\operatorname{id}]$ of step 1.6. Composing the degree isomorphism of step 1.6 with the inverse of $\rho_*$ gives an isomorphism $\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)\cong\mathbb Z$ carrying $[\rho]$ to the degree-one generator, and an isomorphism carries generators to generators, so $\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)$ is infinite cyclic generated by $[\rho]$; in particular $[\rho]\ne0$. [F13, F14, step 1.6, step 10.1, algebra]

12.1 The clutched bundle over $S^4$ is nontrivial. By [F16] with $n=3$ and $k=4$ the clutching construction applied to $\rho$ produces an oriented rank-three real vector bundle $E_\rho\to S^4$, and the classification of [F16] identifies the isomorphism class of $E_\rho$ with the homotopy class of $\rho$. If $E_\rho$ were trivial it would be isomorphic to $E_c$ for a constant $c$ by step 1.8, so by that classification $\rho$ would be homotopic to the constant map $c$, which step 10.2 excludes. Hence $E_\rho$ is nontrivial, and with step 11.1 this completes the proof of all four clauses of the statement. The argument selects only single vectors in steps 1.3 and 3.2 and finite data elsewhere, so no choice principle is used. [F16, step 1.8, step 10.2, step 11.1, algebra] ∎
